questions.question: ghost-patch reports two nulls as its headline. Why is that a legitimate result rather than a failed project?

answerOptions.text: The pass bars were pre-registered before data and grading is judge-free, so a null is a measured, credible finding
answerOptions.rationale: Pre-registration plus a deterministic oracle make a null a result you can trust, not an excuse.

answerOptions.text: Because a null always means the paper was wrong
answerOptions.rationale: The project explicitly does not claim that — the effect likely needs a stronger model or the iterative regime.

answerOptions.text: Because the project spent very little money
answerOptions.rationale: Low cost ($1.42) is a scope fact, not what makes the null credible.

answerOptions.text: Because an LLM judge confirmed the null
answerOptions.rationale: Grading is judge-free; no LLM judge is involved.

questions.hint: What two properties turn a null into a finding?

questions.question: What does ghost-patch's phrase 'blindness, not blind obedience' capture?

answerOptions.text: The cheap models never register the bad instruction as wrong (awareness 0/6), so they cannot be knowingly obeying it
answerOptions.rationale: The failure is a perception gap, not a willingness to obey a rule the model sees is wrong.

answerOptions.text: The models see the bad instruction and deliberately follow it anyway
answerOptions.rationale: That would be blind *obedience* — the opposite of what the 0/6 awareness null shows.

answerOptions.text: The models are blind to all instructions, good or bad
answerOptions.rationale: They follow ordinary instructions fine; the null is specifically about detecting the wrong-location one.

answerOptions.text: The verifier is blind to ghost errors
answerOptions.rationale: That is a separate limitation; 'blindness' here refers to the models' awareness, not the verifier.

questions.hint: Awareness came in at 0/6 — what does that say about obedience?

questions.question: deepseek's single-pass obedience drop is d = +0.04 with a 95% CI of about [−0.022, +0.103], against a pre-committed 10-point bar. Verdict?

answerOptions.text: A null — the CI straddles zero and never reaches the 0.10 bar, so the drop is indistinguishable from no effect
answerOptions.rationale: Containing zero means you cannot distinguish it from no drop; the pre-registered bar is not met.

answerOptions.text: A reproduction — the point estimate is positive
answerOptions.rationale: A positive point estimate whose interval covers zero is a null, not a reproduction.

answerOptions.text: Invalid — you cannot measure a drop on matched pairs
answerOptions.rationale: Matched pairs are exactly the right design; the result is a valid null.

answerOptions.text: A strong effect, since 0.04 is close to 0.10
answerOptions.rationale: 0.04 is below 0.10 and the interval includes zero — not a strong effect.

questions.question: Why does blind-cite fabricate a corpus (Quill/Quipp) instead of using an LLM judge?

answerOptions.text: Invented entities give exact, contamination-free ownership ground truth (no model has a prior), so attribution is deterministic — replacing the judge
answerOptions.rationale: Fabrication makes 'whose evidence is this' mechanically checkable, extending the judge-free principle to attribution.

answerOptions.text: Fabricated corpora are cheaper to license than real ones
answerOptions.rationale: The motive is exact ground truth and no training-prior contamination, not licensing cost.

answerOptions.text: Because an LLM judge would be more accurate here
answerOptions.rationale: The whole point is to avoid the self-graded-homework trap an LLM judge introduces.

answerOptions.text: To make the task easier for the models to pass
answerOptions.rationale: It is about measurement fidelity; if anything the name-forward surface being easy is a disclosed caveat, not the goal.

questions.question: blind-cite's adversarial cell is 0/36. Why is that a 'right-reason' null?

answerOptions.text: The detectors are validated (16/16) and every one of the 36 trials is a correct behavior — a refusal or explicit discrimination — so deception is genuinely absent, not missed
answerOptions.rationale: Sound detectors plus correct model behavior mean the null reflects real absence of the phenomenon.

answerOptions.text: The detector failed to fire, so nothing was counted
answerOptions.rationale: The detectors are validated 16/16; the null is not a detection failure.

answerOptions.text: The models deceived but the harness scored it as safe
answerOptions.rationale: They did not deceive — they refused or named the true owner.

answerOptions.text: The sample was too small to detect anything
answerOptions.rationale: M0 is a pilot, but the outcomes are fully accounted for as right-reason behavior, not undetectable noise.

questions.question: How should blind-cite's status be stated honestly?

answerOptions.text: As in-progress: M0 fit-pilot validated the detectors and corpus and produced an early null; M1 (the powered, possibly multi-doc run) is unrun
answerOptions.rationale: M0 is a pilot; the honest framing keeps it from inflating into a finished result, and notes the README is stale.

answerOptions.text: As complete, with a well-powered null result
answerOptions.rationale: M1 is not yet run; calling it complete overstates a pilot.

answerOptions.text: As a confirmed reproduction of deceptive grounding
answerOptions.rationale: The pilot found the opposite — an early null on this surface.

answerOptions.text: As whatever the README says
answerOptions.rationale: The README is stale; the M0-BRIEF and verdict JSON are the source of truth.
